extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patentees, opponents, patent attorneys, and other stakeholders interested in EPO appeal procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of procedural standards, requirements and practice for appeals before the Boards of Appeal (including the Enlarged Board) of the European Patent Office under the EPC. Covers admissibility, time limits, scope of review, oral proceedings, remittal, fee reimbursement, independence and related procedural rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appealable decisions (which first-instance decisions may be appealed)
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal may be filed against a decision of a first instance department of the EPO, i.e. a decision of the Receiving Section, of an Examining Division, of an Opposition Division or of the Legal Division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Boards of Appeal are not competent to review decisions taken by the EPO acting as international authority under the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT). Most appeals are against Examining and Opposition Divisions; fewer are against Receiving Section and Legal Division decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits and formal requirements for admissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: For an appeal to be admissible, notice of appeal must be filed at the EPO within two months of notification of the contested decision, and the fee for appeal must be paid. In addition, within four months of notification of the decision, a statement setting out the grounds of appeal must be filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement of grounds shall contain the appellant's complete case (Article 12(3) RPBA 2020). The requirements for admissibility must not only be satisfied when lodging the appeal but must be sustained throughout the duration of the appeal proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adversely affected requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The appellant must be adversely affected by the appealed decision in order for the appeal to be admissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party is only 'adversely affected' if the order of the appealed decision does not comply with its request (i.e., what the party requested during the first-instance proceedings). Example: an opponent who requested revocation of a patent in its entirety is not 'adversely affected' by a decision to revoke the patent in its entirety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspensive effect of appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal has a suspensive effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, filing an appeal against a refusal of a patent application suspends the effect of the order refusing the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory revision in ex parte proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: If an appeal is lodged in ex parte proceedings and the first-instance department regards the appeal as admissible and well founded, it must rectify its decision (interlocutory revision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interlocutory revision is useful for procedural expediency and economy, e.g. where amendments filed with the appeal clearly overcome first-instance objections. If not allowed within three months of receipt of the statement of grounds, the case must be transferred to the Board of Appeal without delay. If an interlocutory revision occurs, the appeal fee may be reimbursed in full if such reimbursement is equitable by reason of a substantial procedural violation. If the first-instance department grants interlocutory revision but refuses reimbursement of the appeal fee, it must remit the reimbursement request to a Board of Appeal (it is not competent to refuse such a request).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of admissibility at every stage
rubrics_metrics.description: The admissibility of an appeal may be assessed at every stage of the appeal proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissibility requirements must be sustained throughout the proceedings (approximately until a decision is issued in written proceedings or delivered at oral proceedings). A Board may choose to leave open the question of admissibility in certain circumstances (e.g., if none of the appellant's requests are considered allowable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and standard of review on the merits (full review)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an appeal is admissible, the Board of Appeal examines whether the appeal is allowable, i.e. the Board addresses the merits of the case. The boards have competence to review appealed decisions in full, including points of law and fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing discretionary first-instance decisions (for example admitting late-filed facts/evidence under Article 114(2) EPC), the Board should only overrule such a decision if the department applied the wrong principles, took no account of the right principles, or exercised its discretion in an unreasonable way, thus exceeding proper limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional remittal to the first instance
rubrics_metrics.description: After examining allowability, a Board has the discretion to either exercise any power within the competence of the department responsible for the appealed decision or remit the case to that department for further prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards may remit to give parties the possibility of defending their case before two instances, but there is no absolute right to a two-instance decision. Boards generally consider procedural efficiency and the need to bring proceedings to a close within an appropriate period when deciding whether to remit. As a rule, the Board shall not remit unless special reasons present themselves (fundamental deficiencies that are apparent in the first-instance proceedings may constitute such special reasons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceleration of proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeal proceedings may be accelerated by giving a case priority over others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party may request accelerated processing; such a request must be reasoned. The Board has discretion to grant or refuse the request. Courts, competent authorities of contracting states, and the Unified Patent Court may also request acceleration (without providing a specific reason). The Board may also accelerate proceedings of its own motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral proceedings (right, publicity and preparation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral proceedings in appeal may take place at the request of the EPO or any party; they are held in Haar or Munich and are public unless very particular circumstances apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral proceedings are a specific and codified part of the right to be heard (Article 113(1) EPC). Oral proceedings may be held by videoconference. To prepare, the Board shall issue a communication drawing attention to matters of particular significance and may provide a preliminary opinion. A decision may be announced at the end of oral proceedings; oral proceedings aim to reach a conclusion on the case. A list of public oral proceedings is available on the EPO website.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial procedural violation and reimbursement of appeal fee
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Board of Appeal finds that a substantial procedural violation occurred during first-instance proceedings and considers the appeal allowable, the appeal fee shall be reimbursed if such reimbursement is equitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of substantial procedural violation include violation of the right to be heard (Article 113(1) EPC) or a decision not properly reasoned (Rule 111(2) EPC). To be properly reasoned, a decision must 'contain, in logical sequence, those arguments which justify its order' so as to enable parties and the Board to examine whether the decision was justified. More generally, a substantial procedural violation is an objective deficiency affecting the entire proceedings and means that procedural rules were not applied as prescribed by the EPC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reimbursement of appeal fee upon withdrawal of appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The appeal fee is reimbursed in full if the appeal is withdrawn before filing the statement of grounds and before the period for filing that statement has expired; partial reimbursement is possible at later stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial reimbursement may be at rates of 75%, 50% or 25% depending on the stage at which the appeal is withdrawn. The withdrawal of an appeal must be explicit and unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binding character and precedential value of Boards' decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPC system does not treat established jurisprudence as binding; there is no principle of binding case law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Board of Appeal decision is binding only on the department whose decision was appealed insofar as the facts are the same. If a Board considers it necessary to deviate from earlier Board decisions, it must give grounds for the deviation unless in accordance with an earlier decision/opinion of the Enlarged Board. A decision of the Enlarged Board of Appeal is binding only on the Board of Appeal in respect of the appeal in question (i.e., the referring Board). Outside the EPO, Boards' decisions are not strictly binding on national courts but have persuasive authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of a Board's decision under Rule 140 EPC
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Rule 140 EPC, only linguistic errors, errors of transcription and obvious mistakes may be corrected in decisions of the EPO, including decisions of the Boards of Appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correction is limited to those categories; the possibility to correct a decision is available for Boards' decisions as well as other EPO decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence and appointment/removal of Board members
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the Boards of Appeal and of the Enlarged Board are appointed by the Administrative Council on a proposal from the President of the EPO and have a five-year term; removal during the term is only on serious grounds under Article 23(1) EPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board members are considered 'judges in all but name' and are only bound by the European Patent Convention (not by the Guidelines for Examination). They have a duty of independence. There have been calls for greater institutional independence (e.g., a separate judicial body) and proposals (e.g., lifetime appointment) that would require revision of the EPC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case referencing system for Boards of Appeal decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Each decision of the Boards of Appeal and the Enlarged Board of Appeal has an alphanumeric reference (e.g., T 285/93). The initial letter indicates the type of board (G, R, T, J, D, W, 'Art. 23').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The number before the slash is a serial number allocated chronologically at DG3; the last two digits indicate the year of receipt of the appeal in DG3. The letter 'V' is sometimes used to refer to a decision of an Examining or Opposition Division. Decisions are also sometimes referred to by date to distinguish different decisions in the same case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remittal: 'special reasons' rule (RPBA/Article 11 guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Boards normally will not remit a case to the department whose decision was appealed for further prosecution unless special reasons present themselves for doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a rule, fundamental deficiencies apparent in the proceedings before the first-instance department constitute such special reasons. Article 11 RPBA 2020 and Rule 103(1)(a) EPC provide related guidance: remittal is exceptional and aims to balance parties' rights to two-instance consideration against procedural efficiency.
